question: A shaper is best described as a…
options: Rotating machine tool using an abrasive wheel
Reciprocating machine tool using a single-point tool
Spark-erosion machine using a wire electrode
Rotating machine tool using a multi-point cutter
explanation: The shaper is a reciprocating machine tool; the ram carries a single-point tool to and fro.

question: In a shaper, the rotary motion of the motor/bull gear is converted into…
explanation: The drive mechanism converts rotary motion into the reciprocating motion of the ram.

question: Which surfaces does a shaper mainly produce?
options: Flat surfaces — horizontal, vertical or inclined
Internal bores of very small diameter
Helical threads on long round bars
explanation: Shapers produce flat surfaces in any orientation, plus slots and grooves.

question: On a shaper, metal is cut during…
explanation: Cutting takes place only in the forward stroke; the return stroke is idle.

question: The return stroke of a shaper is called the idle stroke because…
options: No metal is removed during it
The tool is changed during it
The ram does not move during it
The motor is switched off during it
explanation: No cutting takes place on the return stroke, so it is wasted (idle) time.

question: The purpose of the quick-return mechanism in a shaper is to…
options: Reverse the direction of the cross feed
Make the cutting stroke faster than the return
Increase the depth of cut per stroke
Reduce the time lost on the idle return stroke
explanation: A quick-return mechanism makes the return stroke faster, reducing total machining time.

question: Most shapers use which quick-return mechanism?
explanation: The lecture states most shapers use the crank and slotted-lever quick-return mechanism.

question: How does shaping differ from planing?
options: Shaping uses a multi-point cutter; planing does not
In shaping the work reciprocates; in planing the tool does
In shaping the tool reciprocates; in planing the work does
Shaping is used only for round work
explanation: In a shaper the ram (tool) reciprocates over fixed work; in a planer the table (work) reciprocates under a fixed tool.

question: Machining is a metal-removal process in which metal is removed…
options: By pressing it into a die
By melting with an electric arc
In the form of chips by a cutting tool
By adding a thin plated layer
explanation: Machining removes metal as chips with a suitable cutting tool to get the desired size and shape.

question: In metal cutting, the chip thickness compared with the uncut chip thickness is…
explanation: The chip is plastically deformed (compressed) while shearing, so it is thicker than the uncut layer.

question: The two relative motions needed in a machine tool are…
explanation: Primary motion gives the cutting velocity; secondary motion feeds the tool to the uncut portion.

question: In generating a flat surface on a shaper, the generatrix is the line produced by the…
options: Down feed of the tool head
explanation: Generatrix = line traced by the primary (cutting) motion; directrix = line traced by the secondary (feed) motion.

question: On a shaper, the directrix is the line produced by the…
explanation: The crosswise feed of the table traces the directrix; the ram stroke traces the generatrix.

question: In orthogonal cutting, along which plane is metal sheared ahead of the tool?
explanation: The notes sketch the shear plane ahead of the tool where the chip forms; the rake angle is measured on the tool face.

question: Which of these is NOT a part of the crank and slotted-lever mechanism?
explanation: Parts: bull gear (crank), crank pin, sliding block, slotted lever, pivot, link to ram, driving pinion. The index plate is part of a milling dividing head.

question: In a crank shaper, the bull gear is driven by…
options: A small driving pinion from the motor
The ram through the connecting link
The table cross-feed screw and ratchet
The clapper box through its hinge pin
explanation: A driving pinion (driving gear) from the motor drives the large bull gear.

question: In the quick-return mechanism, the sliding block…
options: Is fixed to the ram and slides in the column
Clamps the work in the vice
Rides on the crank pin and slides in the slotted lever
Holds the tool in the clapper box
explanation: The sliding block on the crank pin slides in the slot, making the lever oscillate about its pivot.

question: In the ME-106 shaper wall chart, the crank turns through how many degrees during the cutting stroke?
explanation: The chart shows 240° of crank rotation for the cutting stroke and 120° for the return stroke.

question: If the cutting stroke takes 240° of crank rotation and the return stroke 120°, what is the ratio of cutting time to return time?
explanation: At constant crank speed, time ∝ angle: 240/120 = 2, so cutting takes twice as long as return.
ref: Manufacturing notes p.19; Shaper wall chart

question: The quick-return ratio (cutting time : return time) of shapers usually lies between…
explanation: Typical quick-return ratios are between about 1.5 and 2.

question: On a crank shaper, the length of stroke is changed by…
options: Moving the table on the cross rail
Changing the number of teeth on the pinion
Changing the crank-pin radius on the bull gear
explanation: Moving the sliding block (crank pin) nearer to or farther from the bull-gear centre changes the stroke length.

question: The position of the stroke (where the ram works relative to the job) is adjusted by…
options: Changing the crank-pin radius on the gear
Changing the speed of the main motor
Shifting the ram relative to its link and locking it
Raising or lowering the cross rail
explanation: The ram is moved relative to its connection and locked with the ram locking handle, without changing the stroke length.

question: In a crank and slotted-lever mechanism, the crank radius is 100 mm and the distance from the crank centre to the lever pivot is 200 mm. What is the ratio of cutting time to return time?
explanation: cos θ = r/d = 0.5, θ = 60°. Return angle = 2θ = 120°, cutting = 240°, so ratio = 240/120 = 2.
ref: Theory: Hajra Choudhury; Manufacturing notes p.19

question: For a shaper, the return stroke takes 144° of crank rotation. What is the cutting-to-return time ratio?
ref: Theory: Hajra Choudhury; Manufacturing notes p.19

question: A shaper ram makes 30 double strokes per minute with a 240° : 120° quick return. How long does one cutting stroke take?
explanation: One double stroke = 60/30 = 2 s. Cutting = 240/360 × 2 = 1.33 s; return = 0.67 s.
ref: Shaper wall chart; Manufacturing notes p.19

question: The cutting speed of a shaper is given by…
explanation: L = stroke length (mm), N = double strokes/min, m = return time/cutting time. πDN/1000 is for turning.

question: A shaper has a stroke length of 150 mm, makes 40 double strokes per minute and has m = return time/cutting time = 0.5. What is the cutting speed?
explanation: V = L·N·(1 + m)/1000 = 150 × 40 × 1.5 / 1000 = 9 m/min. Ignoring (1 + m) gives 6 m/min.

question: The 38 mm wide face of the ME-106 block is shaped with a cross feed of 0.5 mm per double stroke. How many double strokes are needed for one pass?
explanation: Number of strokes = width/feed = 38/0.5 = 76.
ref: Theory: Hajra Choudhury; Log Sheets ME-106 p.3

question: If the shaper makes 38 double strokes per minute, how long does it take to cover the 38 mm wide face of the ME-106 block once at 0.5 mm feed per double stroke?
explanation: Strokes = 38/0.5 = 76; time = 76/38 = 2 min.
ref: Theory: Hajra Choudhury; Log Sheets ME-106 p.3

question: Which part of a shaper carries the tool head and reciprocates?
explanation: The ram reciprocates in the column guides and carries the tool head at its front.

question: Which part of the shaper is mounted at the front of the ram and can be swivelled for angular cuts?
explanation: The tool head on the front of the ram can be swivelled to cut inclined surfaces (wall chart: "head can swing on front of the ram").

question: On a shaper, the depth of cut is given by the…
options: Down-feed screw (handle) on the tool head
Ram locking handle on the ram
explanation: The down-feed screw lowers the tool slide by the required depth.

question: What is the function of the clapper box on a shaper?
options: Gives the cross feed to the table every stroke
Sets the length of the ram stroke for the job
Lets the tool lift on the return stroke so it does not drag
Holds the work firmly on the table during cuts
explanation: The clapper block is hinged, so the tool swings up on the return stroke and does not rub the work.

question: On a shaper, the table is carried on the…
options: Cross rail on the front of the column
Ram at the top of the column
Tool head at the front of the ram
explanation: The table is mounted on the cross rail; the cross-feed screw moves it sideways and the rail can be raised or lowered.

question: Which part houses the drive mechanism and carries the ram guides?
explanation: The column is a hollow box casting on the base that houses the bull gear mechanism and supports the ram.

question: Which part steadies the front of the shaper table?
explanation: The front support for the table (shown on the wall chart) prevents the table from sagging under cutting forces.

question: How is the job held on the shaper in the ME-106 lab?
options: On a magnetic chuck on the table
In a machine vice on the table
In a three-jaw chuck on the ram
explanation: The notes say to lock the workpiece in the plain machine vice; the log sheet says to fix it tightly using the clamp.

question: Which set of parts is shown on the "Parts of a standard shaper" chart in the ME-106 lab?
options: Ram, clapper box, tool, table and front support
Wheel head, magnetic chuck and dogs
explanation: The wall chart labels the head (swivelling on the ram), clapper box, tool, ram, table and front support for the table.

question: Which of these parts is NOT found on a shaper?
explanation: Lead screw and half-nut are lathe threading parts. Shapers have a ram, tool head, clapper box, table, cross rail, column and base.

question: Shapers classified by the mechanism that drives the ram are…
explanation: By ram drive: crank, geared, hydraulic. By table: standard, universal. By ram position: horizontal, vertical, travelling head. By stroke: push, draw.

question: Shapers classified by the design of the table are…
explanation: A universal shaper's table can be swivelled and tilted; a standard shaper's cannot.

question: Horizontal, vertical and travelling-head shapers are classified by…
options: Position and travel of the ram
explanation: This classification is by the position and travel of the ram.

question: Shapers classified by the type of cutting stroke are…
explanation: In a push type the tool cuts as the ram moves away from the column; in a draw type it cuts on the stroke towards the column.

question: In a push-type shaper, cutting takes place when the ram moves…
explanation: Push type (most common): cuts on the outward stroke. Draw type: cuts on the stroke towards the column.

question: The single-point cutting tool used on the shaper in the ME-106 lab is made of…
explanation: The shaping log sheet lists a single-point cutting tool made of high-speed steel.

question: Which of these is NOT a part of a single-point cutting tool (as in the shaping slides)?
explanation: Parts: shank, face, base, heel, nose, side and end cutting edges, major and minor flanks. Tang is part of a file.

question: Which property lets a cutting tool keep its hardness at high cutting temperatures?
explanation: Cutting-tool properties: hot hardness, toughness, wear resistance, chemical stability, shock resistance, low friction, favourable cost.

question: Which of these is NOT a desirable property of a cutting-tool material?
explanation: Low friction is desirable, along with hot hardness, toughness, wear resistance, chemical stability and shock resistance.

question: Which list of cutting-tool materials is in order of increasing hot hardness?
options: HSS → carbon tool steel → ceramic → cemented carbide
Carbon tool steel → HSS → cemented carbide → ceramic
Ceramic → cemented carbide → HSS → carbon tool steel
Cemented carbide → carbon tool steel → ceramic → HSS
explanation: Hot hardness rises from carbon tool steel to HSS, carbides, ceramics, CBN and diamond.

question: Which of these is a cutting-tool material listed in the shaping slides?
explanation: The slides list carbon tool steel, HSS, cemented carbide, ceramic, CBN and diamond.

question: Why are shaper tools made more robust, with smaller rake angles, than lathe tools?
options: They are made of a softer grade of steel
They cut on both the forward and return strokes
They take an impact at the start of every cutting stroke
They never actually touch the workpiece
explanation: Shaping is an intermittent cut: the tool strikes the work at the beginning of each stroke, so it needs a strong edge.

question: What is the objective of the ME-106 shaping job?
options: To turn a mild-steel bar down to Ø38 mm
To grind a flat face to a fine finish
To cut a 22-tooth spur gear on a disc
To reduce a block to 38 mm × 21 mm × 73 mm
explanation: The shaping log sheet objective: reduce the given block to the desired dimensions 38 × 21 × 73 mm.

question: What is the finished LENGTH of the ME-106 shaping block?
explanation: The block is 73 mm long, 38 mm wide and 21 mm high.

question: What is the finished HEIGHT (thickness) of the ME-106 shaping block?
explanation: Height (thickness) = 21 mm; width = 38 mm; length = 73 mm.

question: What is the finished WIDTH of the ME-106 shaping block?
explanation: Width = 38 mm.

question: What is the volume of the finished ME-106 shaping block?
explanation: 73 × 38 × 21 = 58 254 mm³. (132 mm is just the sum of the three dimensions.)

question: Which tools are listed on the ME-106 shaping log sheet?
options: Index plate, mandrel, catch pin, worm wheel, shaft and rough flat file
HSS tool, scale with stand, marking block, try square, hammer, chalk, dot punch
Wire electrode, dielectric supply, clamping wire, power supply and part program
Emery paper, pumice powder, copper wire, polishing machine and solution
explanation: The shaping log sheet lists the HSS single-point tool, scale with base (stand), marking block, try square, hammer, chalk and dot punch.

question: Which marking tool is used in the ME-106 shaping lab to check that edges are at 90°?
explanation: The try square (written "tri-square" on the log sheet) is used while marking the block.

question: In the ME-106 shaping lab, the dot punch and hammer are used to…
options: Give the depth of cut to the tool
Hold the block firmly in the vice
Make the marked lines permanent and clear
Change the stroke length of the ram
explanation: After chalk-and-scale marking, punching makes the marking clear (notes: "punching to make marking clear").
ref: Log Sheets ME-106 p.3; Manufacturing notes p.21

question: What was the least count of the down-feed scale (the wheel above the tool head) on the ME-106 shaper?
explanation: The shaping log sheet notes L.C. = 0.05 mm for the scale wheel above the head.

question: With a down-feed least count of 0.05 mm, how many divisions lower the tool by 1 mm?
explanation: 1 mm / 0.05 mm = 20 divisions.

question: What is the correct order of the shaping procedure given in the ME-106 notes?
options: Lock job in vice → start machine → chalk & marking → punching → give depth → align with cross feed
Chalk & marking → punching → lock job in vice → align with cross feed → give depth → start machine
Punching → chalk & marking → give depth → start machine → lock job in vice → align with cross feed
Start machine → give depth → chalk & marking → lock job in vice → punching → align with cross feed
explanation: Notebook procedure: 1 chalk & marking, 2 punching, 3 lock the job in the plain machine vice, 4 align with the cross-feed handle, 5 give depth with the depth handle, 6 start the machine.

question: What is the FIRST step of the ME-106 shaping procedure?
options: Start the machine with the black button
Mark the dimensions on the block
explanation: Step 1: mark the dimensions using the scale with stand, marking block, try square, hammer and dot punch.
ref: Log Sheets ME-106 p.3; Manufacturing notes p.21

question: After marking, the block is…
explanation: Step 2: configure the machine so the block fits tightly using the clamp (vice).

question: In the ME-106 procedure, how is the tool first brought up to the block?
options: Using the ratchet-and-crank feed until the tool just touches
By starting the ram at full speed and waiting
By lowering the head 2 mm at once onto the block
By swivelling the tool head 90° towards the block
explanation: Step 3: using the ratchet and crank mechanism, bring the tool near the block so they just touch.

question: For the first cut in the ME-106 shaping job, the tool head is lowered by…
explanation: Step 4: using the wheel above the head, bring the head and tool down by 1 mm on the scale.

question: In the ME-106 shaping job, by how much is the head lowered for later cuts?
explanation: Step 6: after the first removal, bring the head down again by 0.5–1 mm as required (with the machine off).

question: In the ME-106 shaping procedure, when is the depth of cut increased?
options: Only after all sides are done
While the ram is moving fast
explanation: The log sheet says the head is brought down again with the machine turned off.

question: How is the ME-106 shaping machine started?
options: By turning the bull gear by hand
explanation: Step 5: start the machine using the black button.

question: After one side of the block reaches size, what is done next?
options: Leave the machine running and turn the block
Switch off, remove waste, then repeat for the other sides
Polish the side with a file only
explanation: Steps 7–9: once one side is at size, turn off the machine, remove waste, remove the block and repeat steps 2–8 for the other sides.

question: Why must the crank on the ratchet be readjusted while shaping?
options: So the table feeds in the correct direction during the run
So the ram stroke becomes longer with each pass
So the vice opens automatically after each cut
So the tool lifts on the cutting stroke instead
explanation: The log sheet: always readjust the crank on the ratchet so the base (table) moves in the correct direction while the machine runs.

question: In the ME-106 notes, which handle is used to align the job with the tool before cutting?
explanation: Notes step 4: use the cross-feed handle to align the work with the tool; step 5: use the depth handle to give depth of cut.

question: In the ME-106 notes, which step comes immediately BEFORE starting the machine?
options: Giving the depth of cut with the depth handle
explanation: Order: … align with cross feed → give depth with depth handle → start machine.

question: A face needs 2 mm removed. The first cut is 1 mm and later cuts are 0.5 mm each. How many cuts are needed in total?
explanation: 1 mm (first cut) + 0.5 + 0.5 = 2 mm, so 3 cuts.

question: While the shaper is running, you should never…
options: Put your hands on the machine
Keep the area clear of chips
explanation: Precaution 2: never put hands on the machine while it is turned on.

question: After touching the block, the head should NOT be lowered by more than about…
explanation: Precaution 3: the head should not be brought down more than 2 mm after touching the block (too deep a cut can break the tool).

question: Which precaution about the ratchet appears on the ME-106 shaping log sheet?
options: Oil the ratchet while the cut is on
Keep the ratchet disengaged at all times
Ensure the table moves in the correct direction
explanation: Precaution 4: ensure the ratchet system is configured so the base moves in the correct direction.

question: When should the depth of cut be changed on the shaper?
options: Any time, if you are quick
Only when the machine is stopped
During the return stroke at full speed
explanation: The log sheet procedure increases depth with the machine turned off.

question: Before starting a shaper, the stroke length and position must be set so that…
options: The tool touches the vice jaws at each end
The tool stays in the middle of the job only
The tool clears the work at both ends of the stroke
The ram hits the column at the end of return
explanation: The tool must overrun the job slightly at both ends; otherwise it hits the work or the vice.

question: Where should the operator NOT stand while the shaper is running?
options: In front of the ram, in line with its stroke
Beside the table, clear of the ram
At the side where the feed handle is
explanation: Never stand in line with the reciprocating ram.

question: Which of these is NOT a shaping-lab precaution?
options: Lower the head 5 mm per cut to save time
Never put hands on the running machine
explanation: The head must not be lowered more than about 2 mm after touching the block.

question: Which is an advantage of a shaper?
options: It has a very high production rate
It cuts metal on both strokes
Simple, cheap single-point tools and easy set-up
explanation: Shapers use inexpensive single-point tools and are easy to set up for small jobs.

question: Which is a limitation of the shaper?
options: It can only cut round work between centres
It is slow, because it cuts only on one stroke
It needs a diamond tool for every cut
It cannot make flat surfaces at all
explanation: Cutting takes place only in the forward stroke, so production is slow; it suits small or medium jobs.

question: Which job is typically done on a shaper?
explanation: Shapers machine flat horizontal, vertical and inclined surfaces, slots, keyways, V-blocks and dovetails.

question:
Assertion (A): The return stroke of a shaper is made faster than the cutting stroke.
Reason (R): No metal is removed during the return stroke.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
explanation: Both true, and R explains A: since the return stroke is idle, it is speeded up (quick return) to save time.

question:
Assertion (A): The clapper block lifts the tool during the return stroke.
Reason (R): The clapper block is rigidly bolted to the tool head.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
explanation: A is true, R is false: the clapper block is HINGED on a pin, which is what lets it lift.

question: In a shaper, metal is removed on both the forward and return strokes.
explanation: False. Metal is removed only on the forward stroke; the return stroke is idle.

question: In a crank shaper with a 240°/120° split, the return stroke is faster than the cutting stroke.
explanation: True. The return stroke uses only 120° of crank rotation versus 240°, so it takes half the time.
ref: Shaper wall chart; Manufacturing notes p.19

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled A?
explanation: A = Ram. Reciprocating slide that carries the tool head and gives the cutting stroke.
label: A

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled B?
explanation: B = Tool head. Mounted at the front of the ram; can swivel; carries the down-feed slide and clapper box.
label: B

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled C?
explanation: C = Down-feed handle. Lowers the tool to give the depth of cut.
label: C

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled D?
explanation: D = Clapper box. Holds the tool post; its hinged block lets the tool lift on the return stroke.
label: D

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled E?
explanation: E = Cutting tool. Single-point HSS tool that cuts on the forward stroke.
label: E

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled F?
explanation: F = Vice. Holds the job on the table.
label: F

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled G?
explanation: G = Table. Carries the vice and work; moved crosswise for feed.
label: G

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled H?
explanation: H = Cross rail. Mounted on the column front; carries the table and its cross-feed screw.
label: H

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled I?
explanation: I = Column (body). Box casting housing the drive and carrying the ram guides.
label: I

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled J?
explanation: J = Base. Supports the whole machine.
label: J

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled K?
explanation: K = Table support. Front support that steadies the table.
label: K

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled L?
explanation: L = Ram locking handle. Locks the ram after the stroke position has been adjusted.
label: L

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled M?
explanation: M = Driving pulley. Takes power from the motor to drive the bull gear mechanism.
label: M

question: In the figure, which label shows the ram?
explanation: A = Ram. Reciprocating slide that carries the tool head and gives the cutting stroke.
label: A

question: In the figure, which label shows the clapper box?
explanation: D = Clapper box. Holds the tool post; its hinged block lets the tool lift on the return stroke.
label: D

question: In the figure, which label shows the cross rail?
explanation: H = Cross rail. Mounted on the column front; carries the table and its cross-feed screw.
label: H

question: In the figure, which label shows the down-feed handle?
explanation: C = Down-feed handle. Lowers the tool to give the depth of cut.
label: C

question: In the figure, which label shows the ram locking handle?
explanation: L = Ram locking handle. Locks the ram after the stroke position has been adjusted.
label: L

question: In the figure, what is the function of the part labelled D?
options: Lowers the tool to give the depth of cut
Holds the tool post; its hinged block lets the tool lift on the return stroke
Carries the vice and work; moved crosswise for feed
Front support that steadies the table
explanation: D = Clapper box. Holds the tool post; its hinged block lets the tool lift on the return stroke.
label: D

question: In the figure, what is the function of the part labelled C?
options: Reciprocating slide that carries the tool head and gives the cutting stroke
Holds the job on the table
Lowers the tool to give the depth of cut
Takes power from the motor to drive the bull gear mechanism
explanation: C = Down-feed handle. Lowers the tool to give the depth of cut.
label: C

question: In the figure, what is the function of the part labelled H?
options: Holds the tool post; its hinged block lets the tool lift on the return stroke
Front support that steadies the table
Mounted on the column front; carries the table and its cross-feed screw
explanation: H = Cross rail. Mounted on the column front; carries the table and its cross-feed screw.
label: H

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled A?
options: Crank angle for the cutting stroke
explanation: A = Bull gear (crank wheel). Large gear rotating at constant speed; carries the crank pin.
label: A

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled B?
explanation: B = Crank pin. Pin on the bull gear whose radius sets the stroke length.
label: B

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled C?
options: Crank angle for the return stroke
explanation: C = Sliding block. Pivoted on the crank pin; slides in the slot of the lever.
label: C

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled D?
options: Crank angle for the cutting stroke
explanation: D = Slotted lever (link). Oscillates about the pivot, converting crank rotation into ram motion.
label: D

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled E?
explanation: E = Pivot (fulcrum). Fixed point at the lower end about which the slotted lever swings.
label: E

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled G?
options: Crank angle for the cutting stroke
Crank angle for the return stroke
explanation: G = Driving pinion. Small gear from the motor that drives the bull gear.
label: G

question: In the quick-return figure, which label marks the crank angle of the CUTTING stroke?
explanation: H is the larger (240°) arc of crank rotation, so the cutting stroke is the slow one. I is the 120° return arc.
label: H

question: In the figure the crank-pin circle radius is exactly half the distance from the crank centre to the pivot. What is the ratio of cutting time to return time?
explanation: cos θ = r/d = 0.5 → θ = 60°; return = 120°, cutting = 240°; ratio = 2.

question: In the figure, what happens to the stroke length if the crank pin B is moved nearer the bull-gear centre?
options: The return becomes slower than the cut
explanation: A smaller crank-pin radius makes the slotted lever swing through a smaller angle, so the ram stroke is shorter.

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled A?
explanation: A = Clapper box. Housing on the tool head in which the clapper block is hinged.
label: A

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled B?
explanation: B = Hinge pin. Pin about which the clapper block swings forward to lift the tool.
label: B

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled C?
explanation: C = Clapper block. Carries the tool post; seated firmly on the cutting stroke, free to lift on the return.
label: C

question: In sketch 2 of the figure, why has the tool swung up?
options: The depth of cut was increased
On the return stroke the hinged clapper block lifts so the tool does not drag
The tool head was swivelled for an angular cut
explanation: Friction on the return stroke swings the hinged clapper block up, so the tool slides over the work instead of digging in.

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled A?
explanation: A = Shank. Body of the tool, clamped in the tool post.
label: A

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled B?
explanation: B = Face. Top surface over which the chip slides.
label: B

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled C?
explanation: C = Nose. Tip where the side and end cutting edges meet.
label: C

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled D?
explanation: D = Side (major) cutting edge. Main cutting edge along the side of the tool.
label: D

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled E?
explanation: E = End (minor) cutting edge. Cutting edge at the end of the tool.
label: E

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled F?
explanation: F = Major (side) flank. Surface below the side cutting edge.
label: F

question: In the figure, what is the part labelled G?
